targets.name: Avalanche-White Salmon Glaciers
siblings: adams_northwest_ridge = North Face of the Northwest Ridge

targets.approach: Same approach as the standard North Ridge route, via the Killen Creek Trail and PCT.
targets.descent: Descend via the standard North Ridge line.
targets.name: North Ridge (West Face)
siblings: adams_northwest_ridge = North Face of the Northwest Ridge

targets.name: Pinnacle Glacier Headwall
siblings: adams_northwest_ridge = North Face of the Northwest Ridge

targets.approach: From Sedro-Woolley, drive SR 20 east 16 miles to milepost 82, turn north on Baker Lake Highway (FR 11) for about 18 miles, then (after Boulder Creek Campground) turn onto FR 1130 for about 1 mile to FR 1131, and follow it to the Boulder Ridge Trailhead. Hike the Boulder Ridge Trail (maintained about 2 miles to the wilderness boundary), then a steep, unmaintained boot path with a 3rd-class rock band around 3.4 mi/4,700 ft, continuing up the moraine to high camp on the ridge, roughly 5,500-5,900 ft depending on the snowline, just below the Boulder Glacier.
targets.descent: Reverse the route or descend toward Schriebers Meadow
targets.name: Boulder Glacier

targets.approach: Shares the same general approach drainage as the West Route (Jug Creek/Bluff Lake/Cliff Lake benches) to gain the west side of the mountain, then continues around/up to the base of the north ridge rather than the west-ridge saddle system.
targets.descent: Typically descended via the West Route rather than reversing the North Ridge.
targets.descent_text: Parties commonly traverse off the summit and descend the West Route's ramp/heather line rather than downclimbing the North Ridge.
targets.name: North Ridge

adams_avalanche_glacier.approach: From Cold Springs trailhead, traverse via round-the-mountain trail to the southwest side of Mount Adams, approach glacier directly from southwest.
adams_avalanche_glacier.descent_text: From the summit, descend south via the South Spur snowfields (or the snowfield adjacent to the Avalanche/White Salmon glaciers) back toward the Morrison Creek/Cold Springs approach, glissading where conditions allow.
adams_avalanche_glacier.name: Avalanche Glacier

adams_northwest_ridge.approach: Forest Service Road 2329 from Taklakh Lake area (5.7 miles). Killen Creek Trail (#113) to Pacific Crest Trail junction, then High Camp Trail (#10) to meadow camp at 6,900 ft.
adams_northwest_ridge.descent_text: Descend along the North Ridge to the Adams Glacier basin high camp, or in ski-descent conditions the route itself can be down-climbed/skied, threading the same rock-band pinch encountered on the ascent.
adams_northwest_ridge.name: North Face of the Northwest Ridge

wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.approach: Start at the Killen Creek Trailhead (~4,600 ft), accessed via Forest Roads 23, 21, and 2329 from the Randle/Trout Lake side (FR-2329 is frequently snow-blocked into early summer — several parties have had to park lower and walk or bushwhack an extra mile-plus of road/forest to reach the actual trailhead). Follow Killen Creek Trail #113 for about 3.1 miles through subalpine forest and wildflower meadows, gaining moderately, to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 6,100 ft. Cross straight over the PCT onto the High Camp Trail and continue about 1.0 mile further to its end at roughly 6,900 ft, at the edge of the Adams Glacier's lateral moraine — this is the standard High Camp for the route, with some parties pushing slightly higher to sheltered bivy sites (~7,100 ft) in a shallow snow gully just left of the moraine. Total approach is roughly 4 miles and ~2,300–2,500 ft of gain to camp. Killen Creek itself, crossed low on the trail, is the last dependable flowing water; above High Camp plan on melting snow/glacier ice. The trail's tread thins out and becomes a moraine/gully scramble above treeline and is easy to lose in the dark, whiteout, or heavy snow cover — take a GPS
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.descent_text: This is a serious, committing route, not a car-to-car day climb for most parties — plan on a night at High Camp before the climb, then descend all the way to the car on summit day. The Adams Glacier line tops out on the upper mountain near the North Ridge/Suksdorf area close to the true summit (12,276 ft) rather than requiring a full crater traverse. Nearly all parties descend via the North Ridge (the North Cleaver, the broad rock-and-snow rib between the Adams and Lava Glaciers), which closes the loop back to High Camp and the Killen Creek trailhead without a car shuttle. The North Ridge is non-technical (class 2–3) but has a reputation among climbers for being steep, rocky, and longer than it looks from above, with loose, exposed sections; parties describe a short mixed downclimb move or two on verglas-covered rock low on the ridge before it eases into a snowfield that can be plunge-stepped or carefully glissaded back toward camp. No fixed rappel anchors exist on this descent and none are typically needed — treat it as sustained exposed scrambling/downclimbing with an ice axe rather than a rappel descent (0 rappels), though it's worth carrying a rope and a few slings/rock gear as
wa_mount_adams_adams_glacier.name: Adams Glacier

wa_mount_adams_lava_glacier_headwall.approach: Same trailhead and trail as the Lyman Glacier approach: Killen Creek Trail #113 from the Killen Creek Trailhead, about 3.1 miles through lodgepole forest (crossing East Fork Adams Creek near mile 2.5) to the PCT at ~6,100 ft, then the High Camp Trail #10 another 1.0 mile to High Camp/Adams Glacier Meadows (~6,900 ft). From High Camp, the Lava Glacier Headwall is reached more directly than Lyman: traverse off-trail across the lava fields toward the toe of the Lava Glacier without needing to work around Lava Ridge, reaching the base of the headwall (the triangular ice/snow face bounded by the North Ridge on one side and Lava Ridge on the other). This is glacial/talus terrain with crevasse hazard on the glacier itself. Sources consistently stress climbing this face early season — late spring to early summer — since it becomes icy and rockfall-prone as the snowpack recedes later in summer.
wa_mount_adams_lava_glacier_headwall.descent_text: Descend the North Ridge back toward High Camp, the same non-technical but tedious scree/boulder walk-off used for the Adams Glacier and Lyman Glacier routes on this side of the mountain — long, loose volcanic scree, some narrow/exposed sections, and rockfall risk onto other parties, but no rappelling required on the standard line. From High Camp, retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead. The alternative is to continue over the summit and descend the South Climb route to Cold Springs, which lands you at a different trailhead and requires a shuttle.
wa_mount_adams_lava_glacier_headwall.name: Lava Glacier Headwall

wa_mount_adams_lyman_glacier.approach: From the Killen Creek Trailhead (FS Rd 2329, ~3 miles from Takhlakh Lake), follow Killen Creek Trail #113 through open, dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles in you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows (last reliable easy water before the high basin), then the trees thin as the trail climbs rockier terrain to meet the PCT (Trail #2000) at roughly 6,100 ft, about 3.1 miles from the trailhead. Continue straight across the PCT onto the High Camp Trail #10 for about 1.0 mile to High Camp / Adams Glacier Meadows at the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine (~6,900 ft) — a common base camp. From High Camp the route leaves maintained trail: traverse east/southeast, off-trail across lava fields and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, crossing the toe of the Lava Glacier, to reach the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This traverse is glacier/talus travel with real route-finding, especially in low-snow years — a rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on glacier ice. The Lyman Glacier itself splits around a rock outcrop; the north lobe (original route) and south lobe (40° lower half on unbroken neve/ice, upper half broken by crevasses and serac walls) both lead to
wa_mount_adams_lyman_glacier.descent_text: Standard descent is the North Ridge (also called the North Cleaver) or the adjacent snowfield beside it, dropping back toward High Camp — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. It is the least pleasant part of the trip: long stretches of loose, rotten volcanic scree and boulders, occasional narrow/exposed sections, and a real chance of rockfall onto parties below, so groups should spread out and move quickly through the worst of it. No fixed anchors or rappels are used on the standard line; a short rope-assisted downclimb over an isolated rock band is occasionally used by parties uncomfortable with exposure, but this is improvised, not a bolted or standard rappel. Once back at High Camp, retrace the High Camp Trail and Killen Creek Trail to the trailhead. Some parties instead descend the South Climb route to the Cold Springs trailhead, which requires a car shuttle or a long road walk back to Killen Creek since it's a different trailhead entirely.
wa_mount_adams_lyman_glacier.name: Lyman Glacier

wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.approach: Start from the Bird Creek Road trailhead (~5,700 ft) on the Yakama Reservation side; route-finding across moraines and glacier fields begins around 6,700 ft, reaching Sunrise Camp at 8,300 ft. The Yakama Nation decides each year whether overnight stays are allowed, so plan a single-day push in day-use-only years.
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.descent_text: Reverse the ascent: back down the glacier past Sunrise Camp and out the way you came in to Bird Creek Meadows. Descending the South Spur instead is possible, but it is not a variation on the same day out - it finishes at the Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead on the mountain's south side, reached by an entirely different road system from the Yakama Nation approach this route starts on, so it only works if you have a vehicle waiting there. A party that walks off south without one has left its car on the far side of the mountain.
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.name: Mazama Glacier Headwall

wa_mount_adams_north_ridge.approach: Killen Creek Trailhead (Trail #113, off FR 2329 via FR 23) climbs through forest and meadow ~3.1 mi/1,400 ft to the PCT, then continues to High Camp — roughly 4 mi and 2,300 ft of gain total from the trailhead — the shared base camp for the North Ridge, Adams Glacier, and Northwest Ridge routes.
wa_mount_adams_north_ridge.descent_text: Most parties descend the route itself, back down the North Ridge toward high camp; it is non-technical, mostly Class 2 over loose volcanic scree. Some parties instead carry over and descend the South Climb to Cold Springs, which requires a long car shuttle. Watch crevasses on any glacier descent.
wa_mount_adams_north_ridge.name: North Ridge

wa_mount_adams_south_climb.approach: From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Rd to the Forest Road 23 junction; bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 junction for South Climb, turn left and follow FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, then follow FR 8040 (steep, narrow, sharp switchbacks — no RVs/trailers) for 8.1 miles to its end at the South Climb/Cold Springs trailhead (5,600 ft). The trail follows an old roadbed through the burn scar, enters subalpine forest and meadows, crosses Round-the-Mountain Trail #9 and the PCT, then climbs Crescent Ridge to the base of the summit snowfields.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.descent_text: Retrace the ascent line: cross back over the shallow summit crater, down over Piker's Peak, and descend the broad snow slopes of Suksdorf/Crescent Ridge to Lunch Counter, then follow the old roadbed back to the trailhead. Glissading is common on the lower snowfields in firm-but-soft conditions; watch for exposed rock and runout hazards in late season as snow recedes.
wa_mount_adams_south_climb.name: South Climb (South Spur)

wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. Parties reach it via the Cold Springs/South Climb trailhead (5,600 ft, FS Rd 8040 off FS Rd 80): follow the South Climb Trail #183 about 1 mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail, then instead of continuing north toward Lunch Counter, follow Round the Mountain Trail east below Crescent Glacier onto Yakama Nation land, where a separate tribal permit is required and the trail ends at Hellroaring Canyon; the way on, north around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Klickitat and Wilson glacier basins, is a long off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands. Expect a full day just to reach camp in Avalanche Valley, below the Rusk and Wilson glaciers, before a summit attempt.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.descent_text: The descent reverses back down the South Climb to Cold Springs: after topping out via the headwall, parties traverse over toward the summit plateau and descend the standard South Climb route (non-technical snow/scree walk-off, good glissading in early season) back to Lunch Counter and out to the Cold Springs trailhead — a different, easier line than the ascent. This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. Because the Wilson Glacier Headwall itself is steep snow/ice below cliff bands, a party that needs to bail mid-face rather than finish over the top could reasonably rope down using pickets or V-threads in snow/ice, but this would be an improvised retreat, not a documented standard rappel.
wa_mount_adams_wilson_glacier_headwall.name: Wilson Glacier Headwall

wa_mount_baker_boulder_park_cleaver.approach: Drive Baker Lake Highway to FR1130, then FR1131 to its end at the Boulder Ridge Trailhead (~2,700 ft). Hike the Boulder Ridge Trail #605 — nearly flat through an old clear-cut and timber for about 2 miles to a boggy clearing at the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary — then continue on a rougher user path up steep heather, including a class 3 rock step often protected with a fixed line, to a campsite around 5,700 ft where the ridge meets snow and ice.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_park_cleaver.descent_text: Reverse the cleaver and the lower Boulder Glacier crossing back to the 5,700 ft camp, downclimbing the class 3 step where the fixed line was left, then follow the Boulder Ridge Trail back to the trailhead; expect rockfall exposure near the 9,300 ft buttress on the way down as well as up.
wa_mount_baker_boulder_park_cleaver.name: Boulder–Park Cleaver

wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.approach: From the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,700 ft) at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39), follow Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two miles and take the right-hand climbers' path up the Hogsback moraine to camp near 6,000 ft at the edge of the Coleman Glacier. From camp, rope up and cross the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier heading northeast — roughly 2-3 hours of crevassed travel — and take low-to-moderate snow ramps to the foot of the ridge at about 7,500-7,800 ft. Thin snow bridges over a crevasse maze are the main hazard on this crossing.
wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.name: Cockscomb Ridge

wa_mount_baker_coleman_deming.approach: Coleman-Deming on Mount Baker starts at Heliotrope Ridge TH (about 3,700 ft) via Glacier Creek Road (FS 39). Gain about 2,300 ft over roughly 3 miles through forest and alpine meadows, crossing Grouse, Kulshan, and Heliotrope Creeks to reach Hogsback Camp (6,000 ft). Cross creeks in early morning before afternoon glacial melt surge. From Hogsback, rope up on Coleman and Deming Glaciers (crevasses, route-finding). Roman Wall (~40°) is the crux—steep snow between Deming Glacier and summit plateau. Most parties summit on day two.
wa_mount_baker_coleman_deming.descent_text: This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent - reverse the ascent line. From the summit plateau, descend the Roman Wall carefully (many parties down-climb facing in on the steepest section, especially if icy or in a whiteout), back onto the Deming Glacier, across the Baker-Colfax saddle, and back down the Coleman Glacier icefall to the Hogsback and high camp. Route-finding through the Coleman icefall's crevasse maze is often trickier on descent (softer afternoon snow, sun-cupped and collapsing snow bridges); parties note snowbridges on this stretch have collapsed in late season and required an end-run around crevasses on climbers' left. No technical rappels are used on the standard route in normal conditions - this is graded a basic glacier mountaineering line. From Hogsback, retrace the Heliotrope Ridge Trail back to the trailhead.
wa_mount_baker_coleman_deming.name: Coleman–Deming Glacier

wa_mount_baker_coleman_headwall.approach: Start from the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,700 ft, reached via Glacier Creek Rd 39, which reopened to vehicles all the way to the trailhead in August 2026 after flood repairs; it has washed out before, so check its status with the Mount Baker Ranger District before you go). Trail 677 climbs through old-growth forest and flower-filled avalanche chutes; watch for a couple of unbridged creek crossings that can be awkward early season or after rain. At roughly 2.25 mi the maintained trail forks — the left fork continues to the Coleman Glacier overlook, the right fork is the climbers' path that drops toward the moraine and begins the real work. Past Kulshan Cabin's former site (~4,800–5,000 ft, last reliable running water before camp), the trail climbs steeply up the crest of the lateral moraine known as the Hogsback. Most parties establish high camp somewhere on or near the Hogsback between about 6,500 and 7,200 ft — either on the ridge itself or on the flat benches toward the Black Buttes/Roman Nose — roughly 3–3.5 mi and ~3,000 ft above the trailhead. Above camp there is no water except what you melt. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and cross the broken lower Coleman Glacier
wa_mount_baker_coleman_headwall.descent_text: Descent is via the standard Coleman-Deming route, not back down the headwall, and it is a non-technical walk/downclimb with no rappelling required. From the summit plateau, drop down the Roman Wall — a ~35-45° snow slope that most parties downclimb or glissade in a boot-ski — to the saddle between the Black Buttes and Baker's summit dome. From there continue down onto the lower Coleman Glacier, roping back up for crevasse hazard, and retrace the ascent line (or a lower, more direct crossing) back to high camp. From camp, walk back out the Hogsback moraine crest and Heliotrope Ridge Trail 677 to the trailhead — allow 3-4 hours from summit to camp and another 1.5-2.5 hours from camp to the car, longer if the road washout adds its extra miles. No trip reports for this route describe fixed rappels on the standard descent; parties instead glissade/downclimb the Roman Wall on foot. The one place technical rope work sometimes appears is on-route, not on descent proper: if the final bergschrund below the summit ice cap can't be climbed or downclimbed cleanly, some parties build a quick picket or ice-screw/v-thread anchor to belay or lower across it — this is a crux-mitigation tactic during
wa_mount_baker_coleman_headwall.name: Coleman Headwall

wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.approach: From the Park Butte/Schriebers Meadow Trailhead (~3,360 ft, end of FR 13/Sulphur Creek Road), the route follows Park Butte Trail 603. Cross Sulphur Creek on a footbridge/log crossing near the start (can be a ford in high water), then climb through Schriebers Meadow and forest switchbacks to Morovitz Meadows (about 2.25 miles in). For the Easton Glacier route, leave the Park Butte trail here and bear right onto Railroad Grade Trail 603.2, which climbs the crest of a lateral moraine (the 'railroad grade') with the Easton Glacier dropping away on the right. High camp options are at established sites around 5,600 ft (roughly 3.75 miles from the trailhead) or at Sandy Camp, a cluster of rock-walled tent pads at the moraine's end near 5,900-6,000 ft where the maintained trail effectively ends and glacier travel begins. From Sandy Camp, gain the toe of the Easton Glacier, rope up, and ascend the broad glacier, generally staying climbers' right (east) of the major crevasse bands, to the base of the Roman Wall. Hazards: exposed moraine crest can be loose/exposed in wind, Sulphur Creek crossing can be difficult during peak snowmelt, and there is no reliable water source above Morovitz Meadow
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.descent_text: Non-technical walk-off: reverse the ascent line. From the summit plateau, descend the Roman Wall - a sustained 35-45 degree snow/ice slope that is the crux of the whole route and can be quite icy and rockfall-prone late season; many parties face in and plunge-step or down-climb it carefully - then back down the Easton Glacier to Sandy Camp/high camp, generally retracing the up-track and staying right of the major crevasses. From camp, follow Railroad Grade back down to Morovitz Meadows and out Park Butte Trail 603 to the trailhead. No rappels are used on the standard route; this is one of the two easiest ways up Mount Baker and is regularly guided as a walk-up glacier climb.
wa_mount_baker_easton_glacier.name: Easton Glacier

wa_mount_baker_north_ridge.approach: Shares the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,500-3,700 ft) and the same Trail 677 approach as the Coleman-Deming route: switchback through old growth to the Kulshan Cabin site/treeline fork (~2.25 mi), then up the Hogsback moraine to the standard high camp at ~6,000 ft (about 3 mi and 2,300 ft of gain, 4-5 hours for a laden party). From high camp, the North Ridge approach diverges from Coleman-Deming: rope up and cross the Coleman Glacier heading climbers' left (east), navigating crevasses and icefall, to gain the base of the North Ridge proper on the glacier's true right side. The standard start crosses a double bergschrund via a bridge or narrow snow ramp (can be a difficult, exposed step depending on the season) and climbs a broad 40-degree snow gully to the crest of the ridge. Hazards: crevasse and bergschrund crossing is the technical crux of the approach and is season-dependent (can close out entirely by late summer), icefall exposure on the glacier traverse, and the route sees far less traffic than Coleman-Deming so tracks/bridges may be unbroken.
wa_mount_baker_north_ridge.descent_text: The North Ridge is climbed as an ascent-only line - parties do not reverse it. From the ridge crest, 2.5 to 6 belayed pitches of 60-85 degree alpine ice (hardest near the bottom, closer to WI2-3, easing higher) lead up past a prominent ice cliff/ice bulge around 9,600 ft, the route's steepest and most technical section, then the angle eases onto the upper ice cap; trend climbers' left (east) through crevasses to reach the true summit. Descent is via the standard Coleman-Deming route: head west/southwest across the broad summit plateau, down the Roman Wall headwall onto the Deming Glacier, across the Baker-Colfax saddle, and down the Coleman Glacier icefall back to the Hogsback and high camp, then out via Heliotrope Ridge Trail 677. No rappels are used on the standard descent in normal conditions - parties describe it as a straightforward (if long) glacier walk-down, roughly a few hours from summit to camp for a team already familiar with the terrain. A full round trip (approach + climb + descent) commonly runs 10-14 hours from high camp on summit day, roughly matching the Coleman-Deming route's overall mileage/gain — the North Ridge's extra difficulty comes from the technical ice p
wa_mount_baker_north_ridge.name: North Ridge

wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.approach: From the northeast via Chain Lakes Trail to Ptarmigan Ridge. From Artist Point parking, take Chain Lakes Trail (682) to Ptarmigan Ridge Trail (682.1) junction. Continue about 3 miles west along the ridge to Coleman Pinnacle base, then 0.5 miles to Camp Kiser (~6,000 ft).
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.descent_text: Reverse the ascent: descend the Park Glacier, recross the Rainbow Glacier to camp near the Portals, then walk back along Ptarmigan Ridge to Artist Point, taking the lower line north of Coleman Pinnacle to avoid regaining height. Going down the Coleman-Deming instead ends at Heliotrope Ridge on the far side of the mountain and needs a car shuttle.
wa_mount_baker_park_glacier_headwall.name: Park Glacier Headwall

wa_mount_baker_squak_glacier.approach: From the Park Butte/Schriebers Meadow trailhead area, take the Scott Paul Trail; around 4,600 ft leave the maintained trail for the climbers' path to Crag View camp (~6,500 ft, about 3.5 mi from the trailhead with roughly 3,300 ft of gain).
wa_mount_baker_squak_glacier.descent_text: From the summit, descend the upper mountain via the Easton route, then rejoin the Squak Glacier's descent line back past Sherman Peak to Crag View camp and the trailhead.
wa_mount_baker_squak_glacier.name: Squak Glacier

wa_mount_chaval_scramble.approach: The hike-in starts where FR-16 (Illabot Creek Road) reaches the Arrow Creek switchback (~2,220 ft) — this is the trailhead, not a formal one. A boot/fisherman's path leaves the road roughly 20 yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south (right) bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it's reasonably distinct and has occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned, so expect some searching. Follow it about a mile, then turn right, uphill, at the first significant side creek. The crossing near the confluence can be an easy boulder-hop by late summer or a genuine wet ford in early season, so check flow before committing (it's the approach's main creek-ford hazard). Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder and brush (the worst brush of the day) trending southeast, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000–4,300 ft — this is the route-finding crux of the approach: intermittent cairns/flagging at best, and it's easy to end up in the wrong gully. A GPS track of a prior ascent (or careful use of a described waypoint like Point 4593') is genuinely useful here. The last dependable water is
wa_mount_chaval_scramble.descent_text: Descent is a reversal of the ascent line, not a walk-off in a different direction: downclimb the same diagonal west-face ramp back down to roughly 4,000-4,300 ft, re-enter the gully/cliff-band system, and pick back down through the brush and slide-alder benches to regain Illabot Creek, re-crossing the side creek near the same spot used on the way up before following the fisherman's path back to the Arrow Creek trailhead. There is no cairned or maintained route for most of this, so route-finding is the primary descent hazard — it's easy to drop into the wrong gully in the cliff band, and carrying a GPS breadcrumb of your ascent (or flagging key turns) is standard practice. The heather- and moss-covered rock on the ramp is more hazardous descending than climbing since holds face the wrong way and the exposure reads more obviously on the way down; a short, steep, exposed Class 3 section near the top of the ramp is where a party might reasonably choose to place a hand line, though this is discretionary, not standard practice. This is a Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed anchors, no bolted rappel stations, and no established rappels — crampons are occasionally useful on lingering snow pat
wa_mount_chaval_scramble.name: West Route

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.approach: From the Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24/FS 2419 — the lot has a vault toilet, picnic table, and requires a Northwest Forest Pass), Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is a set of stacked, stairstep switchbacks gaining steadily through forest before the upper-trailhead route merges with the longer lower-trailhead trail (2,600 ft TH, 3.1 mi one-way) at roughly 3,900 ft. From the junction, continue up along the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline (~4,500 ft) around 1 mile in. Here is a well-signed junction where the winter/climbers' route breaks right up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, while the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, many switchbacks having stairstep risers that add to the grade. In summer conditions (roughly July–October) the trail is snow-free and well-cut essentially to the top, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes before the final approach to the 5,944 ft summit — total gain from the Upper TH is 2,444 ft over 1.6 mi one-way. There is no reliable water source on the upper route; carry all the water you
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.descent_text: Descend Trail #812 back to the Upper Trailhead — this is a hike/scramble with a walk-down descent and no rappelling on the standard route (0 rappels, no technical anchors involved). When the upper mountain still holds a firm, continuous snowpack in the chute (common well into early summer most years), the popular and much faster descent line leaves the summer switchbacks and drops directly down the chute below the summit saddle: with an ice axe carried in self-arrest position, this is a well-known glissade losing roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes, with glissaders reportedly hitting 10+ mph on good snow. This is genuinely consequential terrain, not a casual slide — an uncontrolled or involuntary glissade, a fall on hard/icy snow without self-arrest skill, or exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute can cause serious injury, so only glissade in full control and bail to the trail if conditions look icy, rocky, or overly fast. Later in the season, as snow in the chute thins and exposes talus and rock, glissading becomes dangerous rather than fun, and the correct call is to stay on the maintained summer switchbacks for the entire descent. Whichever line is taken above timbe
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Standard Trail (Upper Trailhead, NFR 24)

wa_mount_hinman_hinman_glacier.approach: Park at the Necklace Valley Trailhead (~1,650 ft) at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first ~5 miles are deceptively easy, gaining only about 600 ft as the trail follows the East Fork Foss River through regenerated second-growth forest (logged in the 1930s), entering the Alpine Lakes Wilderness at about 1.5 miles. Around the 5-mile mark the trail crosses the East Fork Foss River on a footlog with a handwire (the river runs high and cold under it in early-season snowmelt, so plan the crossing for morning low flow) and then turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 2,400 ft over the next 3 miles on steep, root-laced switchbacks into Necklace Valley proper. This section is the approach's real crux for tired legs and pack weight. The trail eases again as it reaches Jade Lake (~4,600 ft, ~8-9 miles), then Emerald Lake a quarter mile beyond, then Opal Lake, threading through the swampy, lake-studded Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water throughout, but buggy in early/mid-summer. wa_mount_hinman_hinman_glacier.descent_text: This is a walk-off / downclimb descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line the entire way. From the summit, downclimb the class 2-3 ridge scramble back to the top of the glacier remnant, descend the snow/glacier basin back to La Bohn Gap (watch for softened, sun-cupped snow and any residual crevasse slots in early season), then follow the cairned climbers' path back down through the talus and meadow to La Bohn Lakes/Necklace Basin. Most parties treat this as a multi-day trip (roundtrip totals run 22-26 miles with 5,700-9,000 ft of cumulative gain/loss depending on exact line), descending from the summit back to a La Bohn Lakes or Necklace Basin camp the same day and hiking the remaining ~9-10 miles out to the trailhead — back down through Necklace Basin past Opal, Emerald, and Jade Lakes, down the steep rooty 2,400-ft headwall, back across the East Fork Foss River footlog, and out the long, gentle lower trail — on a subsequent day. No technical rope work is required on the standard route; the notable descent hazards are the same river crossing, loose talus, and glacier-remnant travel encountered on the way in, now tackled with tired legs late in the day.
wa_mount_hinman_hinman_glacier.name: Hinman Glacier / Standard

wa_mount_johnson_standard.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, start on Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 through second-growth and then old-growth forest along the Dungeness River. At about 1 mile, bear right at the signed junction onto the Royal Basin Trail (the left fork continues up-valley toward Boulder Shelter/Constance Pass). The Royal Basin trail then climbs gradually for several miles alongside Royal Creek — the main water source for the approach — crossing it on log/plank bridges more than once; these crossings can run fast and cold during early-season snowmelt (June). Around mile 6 the grade steepens sharply for the push to Royal Lake (7.2 mi, roughly 2,500 ft gained from the trailhead), with the final mile gaining about 500 ft on looser, sometimes-eroded tread. From Royal Lake continue south up-valley on the scramblers'/climbers' path roughly another 0.8 mile and 600 ft to Upper Royal Basin (about 8 mi in, ~5,700 ft), a broad heather-and-tarn basin below Mount Deception's northeast face that most parties use as base camp (NPS wilderness permit and bear canister required; no fires; advance reservations cover June 15–Oct 15). wa_mount_johnson_standard.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb from the summit back to the ~6,900 ft Johnson–Clark notch, then retrace the talus-and-moraine descent down into Surprise Basin and back over its rim to Upper Royal Basin, from which the Royal Basin/Upper Dungeness Trail leads back out to the trailhead. The class 4 terrain near the summit is the crux of the descent as well as the ascent — the rock is loose enough in spots that most reported difficulty on this peak comes from downclimbing it, so face in and test holds on anything above class 3. The summit chimney is downclimbed rather than rappelled; there are no fixed/bolted rappel stations reported on Johnson, so a party that wants a rope on the steepest step, particularly if the rock is wet, must rig it from a natural anchor (horn, chockstone, or slung block) of its own.
wa_mount_johnson_standard.name: Standard Route
